concepts.name: Composition of the Electoral College under Article 54
key_dimensions: Exhaustive list: elected members of both Houses of Parliament + elected members of State Legislative Assemblies
UPSC trap: Nominated members of Parliament and State Legislatures are explicitly excluded
UPSC trap: Members of Legislative Councils (MLCs) are excluded even in states with bicameral legislatures
Comparison with Vice-President's electoral college which includes nominated members of Parliament

concepts.name: Exclusion of Nominated Members from the Electoral College
key_dimensions: Constitutional basis: Article 54 uses 'elected members' — nominated MPs under Articles 80(1) and 331 are excluded
Rationale: Nominated members are not people's representatives, hence lack democratic legitimacy for electing the head of state
UPSC trap: Contrast with Vice-President election under Article 66 where nominated members of both Houses participate
Implication: A nominated Rajya Sabha member (e.g., eminent person) has no vote in Presidential election

concepts.name: Exclusion of State Legislative Council Members (MLCs)
key_dimensions: Article 54 specifies only Legislative Assembly members, not Legislative Council members
Rationale: MLAs are directly elected by the people; MLCs have varied and indirect modes of election
States with bicameral legislatures (e.g., UP, Bihar, Maharashtra): only MLAs participate, not MLCs
UPSC trap: Total electoral college strength calculation must exclude all MLCs

concepts.name: Inclusion of Union Territory Legislative Assemblies after 70th Constitutional Amendment
key_dimensions: Original Article 54 included only State assemblies; 70th Amendment (1992) added elected members of Delhi (NCT) and Puducherry
Constitutional basis: Article 54 amended to include UTs with legislatures
UPSC trap: Not all UTs are included — only those with legislative assemblies (Delhi and Puducherry currently); Jammu & Kashmir's statehood/UT status implications
Jammu & Kashmir: after reorganization in 2019, its Legislative Assembly members participate once assembly elections are held

concepts.name: Value of a Member of Parliament's Vote in the Electoral College
key_dimensions: Formula: Total value of all elected MLAs' votes ÷ Total number of elected MPs
Purpose: To maintain parity between Parliament and all State Assemblies combined
UPSC trap: The value is the same for every MP regardless of which state they represent or which House they belong to
Practical implication: MP vote value changes with each election depending on state assembly compositions

concepts.name: Value of a State MLA's Vote — Calculation Formula
key_dimensions: Formula: Total population of the state ÷ (Total number of elected MLAs × 1000); result rounded to nearest integer
Population figure used: 1971 Census (frozen by 42nd Amendment, extended by 84th Amendment until 2026)
UPSC trap: Different MLAs from different states have different vote values; an MLA from UP has a far higher vote value than one from Sikkim
Deliberate design: Balances larger and smaller states in electing the President

concepts.name: Use of 1971 Census Population Figures and the 'Freeze' Provision
key_dimensions: 42nd Constitutional Amendment (1976) froze the population basis at 1971 Census for MLA vote value calculation
84th Constitutional Amendment (2001) extended the freeze until the first census after 2026
Rationale: To prevent penalizing states that successfully implemented family planning programs
UPSC trap: This is distinct from the delimitation freeze — both use 1971 data but serve different constitutional purposes

concepts.name: Principle of Uniformity and Proportional Representation in the Electoral College
key_dimensions: Article 55(1): So far as practicable, uniformity in scale of representation of different states
Article 55(2): Proportionality between the number of votes an MLA casts and the population of the state
Constitutional design ensures that the President represents all states proportionally, not just populous ones
UPSC trap: 'As far as practicable' — implies it is a directive, not an absolute guarantee; rounding off is permitted

concepts.name: Method of Election: Single Transferable Vote with Proportional Representation
key_dimensions: Article 55(3) mandates election by proportional representation using the single transferable vote (STV) system
Voting is by secret ballot — electors rank candidates in order of preference (1, 2, 3...)
Quota for election: (Total valid votes ÷ 2) + 1 (Droop Quota)
UPSC trap: This is the same method used for Rajya Sabha elections and Vice-President election, but the electoral college is different in each case

concepts.name: Droop Quota and Transfer of Votes Mechanism
key_dimensions: Winning quota = (Total valid votes polled ÷ (Number of seats + 1)) + 1; for President with one seat: (Total votes ÷ 2) + 1
If no candidate secures quota in first count, candidate with fewest votes is eliminated and their votes redistributed
Process continues until one candidate crosses the quota
UPSC trap: The quota is based on valid votes polled, not total votes in the electoral college — abstentions reduce the quota

concepts.name: Total Strength of the Electoral College — Numerical Overview
key_dimensions: Elected MPs: 543 (Lok Sabha) + 233 (Rajya Sabha) = 776 elected members
Elected MLAs: Varies across 28 states + Delhi + Puducherry (approximately 4,120+)
Total value of all MP votes = Total value of all MLA votes (parity principle under Article 55)
UPSC trap: Vacancies in the electoral college do not invalidate the election (Article 55(3) proviso)

concepts.name: Effect of Vacancies in the Electoral College on Presidential Election
key_dimensions: Article 71(4) / Article 55(3) proviso: Election of President is not invalidated merely because of vacancies in the electoral college
Vacancies could arise due to deaths, disqualifications, or pending by-elections
UPSC trap: This is a deliberate constitutional safeguard to prevent electoral paralysis
Contrast: Election of Speaker is invalidated if quorum is absent — different rule for different constitutional offices

concepts.name: Parity between Parliament and States in the Electoral College
key_dimensions: Total vote value of all elected MPs = Total vote value of all elected MLAs (by design of the formula)
This ensures Parliament and state legislatures have equal weight in electing the President
UPSC trap: Parity is between totals, not individual MPs and MLAs — an individual MLA may have a higher or lower vote value than an MP
Reflects federal character: President is head of both the Union and the states

concepts.name: Presidential Election vs. Vice-Presidential Election — Electoral College Comparison
key_dimensions: President (Article 54): Elected members of both Houses of Parliament + elected members of State/UT Assemblies
Vice-President (Article 66): Members of an electoral college consisting of members of BOTH Houses of Parliament (elected AND nominated); state assemblies excluded entirely
UPSC trap: VP electoral college is larger in terms of membership categories (includes nominated) but smaller in geographic scope (no states)
Key difference: VP election has no state representation, making it purely a parliamentary affair

concepts.name: Role of Returning Officer and Election Commission in Presidential Election
key_dimensions: Presidential election is conducted by the Election Commission of India under Article 324
Returning Officer is typically the Secretary-General of Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha (alternates)
Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952 governs the procedural aspects
UPSC trap: Unlike general elections, there is no 'Model Code of Conduct' as such; the process is purely an electoral college vote

concepts.name: Dispute Resolution in Presidential Elections — Article 71
key_dimensions: Article 71: All doubts and disputes arising out of or in connection with the election of the President shall be decided by the Supreme Court
Supreme Court's decision is final; election can be declared void by Supreme Court
UPSC trap: Unlike Parliamentary election disputes (High Court jurisdiction), Presidential election disputes go directly to the Supreme Court
Article 71(2): Acts done by President before Supreme Court declares election void remain valid (de facto doctrine)

concepts.name: Eligibility Conditions of Candidates and Their Interaction with Electoral College
key_dimensions: Article 58: Must be Indian citizen, 35 years of age, and qualified for election as Lok Sabha member
Must not hold any office of profit (Article 58(2)) — serving President, VP, Governors, Union/State Ministers are exempt
UPSC trap: A sitting MLA or MP can contest Presidential election but must vacate their seat upon election as President
Nomination: Must be proposed by 50 electors and seconded by 50 electors from the electoral college

concepts.name: Security Deposit and Nomination Process for Presidential Election
key_dimensions: Candidates must submit a security deposit of ₹15,000 to the Reserve Bank of India
Nomination must be subscribed by at least 50 proposers and 50 seconders (all must be members of the electoral college)
UPSC trap: The 50+50 requirement was introduced by amendment to the Presidential and VP Elections Act to prevent frivolous candidates
Original requirement was much lower; raised to reduce the large number of dummy candidates

concepts.name: Federal Character of the Electoral College and Constitutional Design Intent
key_dimensions: The inclusion of state assemblies reflects the quasi-federal nature of India's Constitution
President as constitutional head of Union AND states — hence state legislatures must have a say in election
Parity of vote values between Parliament and states reinforces cooperative federalism
UPSC trap: India does not follow the US model of Electoral College per state; India uses a single national electoral college with weighted votes

concepts.name: Impact of Anti-Defection Law and Disqualification on Electoral College Membership
key_dimensions: A disqualified MP or MLA loses membership of the House and thus ceases to be a member of the electoral college
UPSC trap: A member under disqualification proceedings (not yet decided) still retains voting rights in Presidential election
Members suspended from the House (not disqualified) can still vote in Presidential election — suspension ≠ disqualification
Members on bail after conviction (sentence stayed) retain electoral college membership until final disqualification
